meta.title: Who really said "Death hangs over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — it really is Marcus Aurelius. The line is Meric Casaubon's 1634 translation of Meditations IV.17. Source, Greek original, and translation history verified.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Death hangs over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good'?
meta.ogDescription: A rare authentic one: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations IV.17, in Meric Casaubon's 1634 translation. Greek original and source verified.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine passage from Marcus Aurelius’ Meditations, Book IV.17, in the English translation of Meric Casaubon (first published 1634). The Greek original — “τὸ χρεὼν ἐπήρτηται· ἕως ζῇς, ἕως ἔξεστιν, ἀγαθὸς γενοῦ” — is confirmed on the scholarly readaurelius.org edition ↗, where George Long renders the same line “Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Marcus Aurelius (written c. 170–180 AD, in Greek)
τὸ χρεὼν ἐπήρτηται· ἕως ζῇς, ἕως ἔξεστιν, ἀγαθὸς γενοῦ

source.excerpt: Not as though thou hadst thousands of years to live. Death hangs over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ lists the exact wording — “Death hangs over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good” — as Marcus Aurelius, Meditations IV.17, in the Meric Casaubon translation.
The scholarly readaurelius.org edition of IV.17 ↗ gives the Greek and George Long’s parallel rendering, confirming this is a real passage rather than an internet invention.
Casaubon’s translation was first published in 1634 ↗ as His Meditations concerning himselfe — the earliest complete English version of the work.
source.excerptNote: The popular one-line version usually drops the opening clause (“Not as though thou hadst thousands of years to live”), which is what gives the surviving sentence its urgency.

sourceLink.text: Meditations IV.17 — Greek, Long & modern translations

source.rightsNote: The exact English wording is Meric Casaubon’s translation, first published in 1634 and reprinted many times before 1931; it is firmly in the public domain in the United States. Marcus Aurelius’ original Greek has been public domain for centuries.

author.heading: About Marcus Aurelius
author.bio: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus ruled Rome from 161 to 180 AD, the last of the “Five Good Emperors.” His private notebook, the Meditations, was written in Greek for his own use and never intended for publication; it endures as a foundational Stoic text on mortality, duty, and living well in the present.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: This one is authentic — unusually so for a quote pinned on a “magnet” name. The confusion is not whether Marcus Aurelius said it, but which words and where.

items.who: Meric Casaubon (translator), not Marcus Aurelius verbatim
items.why: Marcus wrote in Greek. “Death hangs over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good” is the phrasing of the 1634 Meric Casaubon translation ↗. Other translators read it differently — George Long: “Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.”

items.who: Cited as both IV.14 and IV.17
items.why: Modern scholarly editions place it at Book IV.17 ↗; some quote sites label it IV.14 because older editions numbered the chapters differently.
The full passage opens “Not as though thou hadst thousands of years to live” — the memento-mori setup that the stand-alone line depends on.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine Marcus Aurelius: Meditations IV.17, in Meric Casaubon’s 1634 English translation ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The Meditations was Marcus Aurelius’ private journal, written in Greek during military campaigns and never meant for anyone else’s eyes. That is what gives lines like this their force: they are an emperor reminding himself, not preaching to an audience.

The thought is pure Stoicism — a memento mori that turns the certainty of death into a reason to act well immediately, rather than a cause for despair. It sits alongside the book’s repeated insistence that the present moment is the only thing anyone actually possesses.
